Sri Lanka’s Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, who produced a world- leading 92.62m in Rome, enters the competition as the man in form.

Article Title: CWG: Jhandu wins bronze as India open Glasgow campaign; Sachin survives tough boxing test
Article Text:
Jhandu Kumar

(WITH INPUTS FROM ARNAB SEAL)

As India slept, Jhandu Kumar hauled the country’s Commonwealth Games campaign onto the medal table.The 28-year-old para powerlifter from Bihar delivered India’s first medal of the Glasgow Games late on Friday, winning bronze in the men’s heavyweight event at the SEC Armadillo. Jhandu finished with 130.9 points after opening with a successful lift of 181kg and improving to 190kg on his second attempt. He then failed to complete 196kg, but his best lift was enough to secure third place.After pressing 190kg, Jhandu sat upright with a smile, thanked God and reached for his wheelchair. His final attempt was agonisingly close, but he could not complete the lift to earn the judges’ approval. He rose smiling nonetheless, though a flicker of disappointment remained as he looked towards his support staff.Jhandu said a technical infringement on the unsuccessful lift had proved costly. “That mistake cost me dearly. Had the lift counted, I would have had a chance to win silver and perhaps even challenge for gold,” he told TOI .Asked whether the occasion had brought additional pressure, Jhandu said, “I had already competed at international events before, so I wasn’t overawed by the occasion. My only focus was to do what I had practised in training and give my best.Small technical mistakes happen in competition, and that’s what happened this time.”In boxing, Sachin Siwach survived a searching test from Canada’s Keoma AlAhmadieh to reach the men’s 60kg round of 16 on Saturday. Al-Ahmadieh troubled the Indian through all three rounds. Sachin, however, landed enough scoring punches to retain a slender edge and secure a 4-1 split-decision victory. He will face England’s Will Hewitt for a place in the quarterfinals on Monday.India’s women endured a difficult Commonwealth Games debut in 3x3 wheelchair basketball, suffering a 16-1 defeat by Wales in their opening Group B match. The Indian team converted only one of its 12 scoring attempts.Lawn bowls, however, supplied another flourish as Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh registered their third successive victory in the women’s pairs competition. The Indians edged Tonga’s Paris Baker and Milika Nathan in a tense tie-breaker after the teams split the opening two sets. Rupa and Pinki won the first set 5-2 before Tonga fought back to take the second 6-4. The Indians then prevailed 2-0 in the tiebreaker to remain unbeaten and stay firmly in the race for a semifinal berth.In the men’s singles event, Putul Sonowal suffered his first defeat as he lost 4-8, 8-9 to Malaysia’s Izzat Shameer Dzulkeple in a crucial Section D clash.
Article Summary: Jhandu Kumar wins bronze in men's heavyweight event at the SEC Armadillo. The 28-year-old para powerlifter from Bihar delivered India's first medal of the Glasgow Games. India's women endured a difficult Commonwealth Games debut in 3x3 wheelchair basketball, suffering a 16-1 defeat by Wales.

Article Title: Once a vegetable seller & e-rickshaw driver, Jhandu now earns spot on CWG podium
Article Text:
Jhandu Kumar

Three years ago, Jhandu Kumar was driving an e-rickshaw through the streets of Harnaut in Bihar ’s Nalanda district to support his family.On Friday night, the 29-year-old completed one of Indian para sport’s most remarkable journeys by winning bronze in the men’s heavyweight para powerlifting event at Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.Jhandu finished with 130.9 points after a best lift of 190kg, becoming India’s first medallist at this edition of the Commonwealth Games. Yet, for the national record holder, the medal meant a lot more than a place on the podium.“Sometimes it’s hard to believe how far I’ve come. But I’m proud that I’ve done something for my country and for Bihar. I had the opportunity to represent India. That gives me immense happiness,” Jhandu told STOI from Glasgow on Saturday.His journey has been defined as much by sacrifice as by success.Affected by polio at the age of five, Jhandu spent years helping his family run their vegetable business at Harnaut Bazaar. Every day he would travel nearly 20km to Bihar Sharif to procure vegetables before returning to sell them in the market. Once the day’s work ended, he would head to Rockstar Gym, where he trained under Gautam Singh.“I first met him in 2019. There was a wedding in a village near mine, and that’s where we met.The moment I saw him, I felt this boy had something special,” recalled Gautam. “Later at his request, in 2020, I opened my gym in Harnaut, and within two months he joined. Since then, we’ve been training together continuously.”The gym soon became Jhandu’s second home, where he spent three to four hours every evening training.Then, when the family’s shop had to be temporarily shut down during the Covid-19, he took up driving an e-rickshaw to support his family.Although he believed it would make life easier, the long hours left him too exhausted to train properly. Despite the challenges, he won his first national medal at National Para Powerlifting Championships in Kolkata in 2022.Convinced that powerlifting was his future, Jhandu eventually sold the e-rickshaw a year later to finance his participation in National Para Powerlifting Championships in New Delhi.Ironically, the gamble appeared to have failed when he was unable to register a successful lift at the competition. But his determination caught the eye of chief national coach Rajinder Singh Rahelu, who invited him to train at Sports Authority of India’s National Centre of Excellence in Gandhinagar.The move transformed his career. Within three years, Jhandu had become one of India’s leading para powerlifters, winning medals at home and abroad, setting the national record in 72kg category with a 206kg lift and earning qualification for Commonwealth Games.There was, however, a hint of disappointment late on Friday in Glasgow as he narrowly missed out on silver, or even gold. Yet standing on the CWG podium was a moment he had dreamt of for years.“This journey was never mine alone. Everyone has played a role in helping me reach this level. Without their support, I don’t think I would have made it this far,” he said. “My journey isn’t over yet. I still have the Asian Games and, hopefully, the Paralympics ahead of me.”Back home in Harnaut, celebrations broke out as family, friends and neighbours rejoiced at the success of the man who once sold vegetables and drove an e-rickshaw to keep his sporting dream alive.“It is a huge achievement. People will see him today as a Commonwealth Games medallist, but very few know how difficult his journey has been,” said Jhandu’s elder brother, Kundan.By afternoon, Kundan had distributed nearly 5kg of ‘Black Atom Bomb’, a popular sweet in the region. And their parents, Ramanand Paswan and Kamala Devi, couldn’t have been happier.“Jhandu spoke to our mother just before the event and she blessed him, saying, ‘Son, wherever you compete, make sure you raise the Indian tricolour.’ Those were her words from the heart, and he has fulfilled that blessing,” said Kundan, who admitted he could barely sleep the entire night out of excitement.His father, who worked as a caretaker at the Bihar State Cooperative Marketing Union’s warehouse for nearly five decades while also selling vegetables, now hopes his son’s achievement will finally help the family secure a shop in the new complex after years of waiting.While the family dreams of a better future, the CWG bronze has also strengthened hopes of an even bigger breakthrough on the international stage.“The govt of Bihar shall provide him with the support needed to train effectively for a successful campaign at LA 2028,” said Raveendran Sankaran, director general-cum-CEO of the Bihar State Sports Authority.For Jhandu, the assurance comes at a crucial stage in his career. After years of funding his own dream — selling vegetables, driving an e-rickshaw and even selling it to continue competing — he now has the backing to chase an even bigger goal — a Paralympic medal in Los Angeles.
Article Summary: Jhandu Kumar won bronze in the men's heavyweight para powerlifting event at Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 29-year-old became India's first medallist at this edition of the Commonwealth Games. Jhandu spent years helping his family run their vegetable business at Harnaut Bazaar.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Mirabai Chanu leads Manipur’s five-pronged medal charge in weightlifting
Article Text:
Mirabai Chanu during the opening ceremony of the Glasgow Commonwealth Games 2026. (PTI Photo)

As the weightlifting competition at Commonwealth Games begins in Glasgow on Sunday, all eyes will be on Mirabai Chanu as she takes the platform in the women’s 48kg category, looking to make it three Commonwealth Games titles in a row.Mirabai has been one of India’s most consistent performers across sports, and the country will be hoping for another memorable display from the Manipuri star as she returns from a career-threatening injury. This time, however, she will not be the state’s only medal hope.Five members of India’s weightlifting squad hail from Manipur, underlining the state’s remarkable dominance in the sport. Watching their progress with immense pride will be veteran coach S Brojendro Singh, who played a key role in the early development of all five, including Mirabai.“It’s a matter of great pride for me. I coached all five of them when they first started weightlifting. Seeing them now represent India at the Commonwealth Games is a huge satisfaction,” Brojendro, who has been coaching at the state sports academy since 2004, told STOI.While Brojendro believes discipline, dedication, sacrifice and unwavering commitment have been central to Manipur’s success in weightlifting, he says Mirabai’s achievements transformed the sport in the state.“Mirabai inspired an entire generation. After people saw what she achieved, many youngsters took up weightlifting believing they too could reach that level. She showed them that it was possible,” he said.One of those inspired by Mirabai is Nirupama Devi, the silver medallist at 2025 Commonwealth Championships, who will make her CWG debut in the women’s 63kg category. Although she earned a place in the junior national camp in 2016, thing didn’t go as planned post 2019.“There were injuries, illness and the Covid-19 break, because of which I was out of national camp. But I kept working hard and now my focus is only on giving my best at CWG,” Nirupama said.Now training under chief national coach Vijay Sharma at Modinagar, she marked her return with a silver medal-winning total of 217kg at the 2025 Commonwealth Championships. Besides her coaches, Nirupama says Mirabai has also played an important role in her development.“Mirabai didi always guides us. Whenever we don’t understand something, she patiently explains it and motivates us. She has always been very supportive,” she said.Another major medal hope is young Martina Devi, who will compete in the women’s +86kg category. After recovering from an ACL injury, she has enjoyed a breakthrough 2026 season, winning both the junior and senior national titles.Bindyarani Devi, who won silver in the women’s 55kg category at Birmingham CWG, has since moved up to the 58kg division. Rishikanta Singh, who narrowly missed the podium in Birmingham, also changed categories to 60kg and heads into Glasgow after winning gold at the 2025 Commonwealth Championships.The entire Indian weightlifting squad, meanwhile, completed its final phase of preparations at University of Wolverhampton’s Walsall Campus, where it trained from June 29 until last week before travelling to Glasgow.The training camp is expected to play a key role as the lifters bid to peak at the right time over the coming days. For Brojendro, however, the medals will tell only part of the story. Watching five lifters who began their journeys under his guidance represent India at the Commonwealth Games is, he says, the greatest reward of his coaching career.
Article Summary: Mirabai Chanu will compete in the women’s 48kg category. The Manipuri star has won three Commonwealth Games titles in a row. Five members of India's weightlifting squad hail from Manipur. Veteran coach S Brojendro Singh played a key role in the early development of all five.

Article Title: CWG 2026 Day 3: No medals for India, but Sachin Siwach advances and Rupa-Pinki stay unbeaten
Article Text:
India's Sachin Siwach, in blue, competes against Canada's Keoma Al-Ahmadieh. (PTI Photo)

Boxing: Sachin Siwach clears opening hurdle



India's Pinki Singh, left, and Rupa Rani Tirkey. (PTI Photo)

Lawn bowls: Rupa-Pinki remain unbeaten, Sonowal suffers first defeat



Artistic gymnastics: India finish fifth in Subdivision 3



Swimming: Indian duo miss 400m freestyle final



Wheelchair basketball: Wales outclass India



Mirabai Chanu headlines India's Sunday hopes



NEW DELHI: India enjoyed another productive day at the Commonwealth Games 2026 on Saturday, with boxer Sachin Siwach advancing to the pre-quarterfinals and the women's lawn bowls pair of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh extending their unbeaten run to stay firmly on course for the semifinals.A day after para powerlifter Jhandu Kumar opened India's medal account with a bronze medal, Indian athletes produced a series of encouraging performances across boxing, lawn bowls and gymnastics, although there were disappointments in swimming and wheelchair basketball.With Olympic silver medallist Mirabai Chanu set to begin her title defence on Sunday, India will look to build on the positive momentum.One of India's brightest medal hopes in boxing, Sachin Siwach, survived a stiff challenge from Canada's Keoma Al-Ahmadieh to progress to the men's 60kg pre-quarterfinals.The 26-year-old prevailed 4-1 in a split verdict in the round of 32 at Glasgow's SEC Centre, overcoming an opponent he had beaten twice before."It was a tough bout but I had beaten him twice before so I was pretty confident," Sachin said. "It was important for me to defeat him today because it was at the Commonwealth Games."Siwach will next face England's William Hewitt in the round of 16.India's women's pairs combination of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh continued their impressive campaign with a third consecutive victory in Section B.The Birmingham 2022 gold medallists defeated Tonga 2-0 in a tie-break after sharing the two sets, strengthening their chances of reaching the semifinals.The Indians won the opening set 5-2 before Tonga bounced back to take the second 6-4. Rupa and Pinki, however, held their nerve in the tie-break to secure victory.The Indian duo now shares three wins from three matches with England but trails the latter on sets won. They will take on Namibia in their fourth sectional match on Sunday.There was disappointment in the men's singles, where Putul Sonowal suffered his first defeat of the campaign.The Assam Police officer lost 0-2 (4-8, 8-9) to Malaysia's Izzat Shameer Dzulkeple despite producing a spirited fightback in the second set after trailing 5-9.Sonowal, who stunned reigning world champion Ryan Bester in his opening match and followed it up with another hard-fought victory, remains second in the Section D standings ahead of his clash against Malta's Shaun James Parnis.India's women's artistic gymnastics team of Pranati Nayak, Nishka Agarwal, Eshita Rewale and Protistha Samanta completed their qualification campaign with a combined score of 29.850 in the floor exercise.The quartet finished with an overall tally of 123.000 points after all four apparatus to place fifth after Subdivision 3 in the women's team and individual qualification competition.The gymnasts had earlier competed in the vault, uneven bars and balance beam before concluding their campaign on the floor.India's challenge in the pool ended early as both Dhakshan Shashikumar and Aryan Nehra failed to progress to the men's 400m freestyle final.Shashikumar clocked 3:58.09 to finish 15th overall among 27 swimmers, while Nehra placed 16th in 4:00.26.Although Shashikumar was seventh midway through his heat, he could not maintain the pace required to qualify.India endured another difficult outing in the women's wheelchair basketball competition, suffering a comprehensive 1-16 defeat to Wales in their Group B fixture.The Indian team struggled to cope with Wales' intensity throughout the contest, converting only one of their 12 scoring attempts as their opponents dominated from start to finish.Attention now shifts to the weightlifting arena, where Olympic silver medallist Mirabai Chanu is expected to launch her Commonwealth Games campaign and begin the defence of her title.India enter the competition despite a disrupted build-up after its weightlifting squad was reduced from 16 to 11 following multiple doping violations, with Dilbag Singh (96kg) the latest lifter to be withdrawn.Even with the setbacks, India remain one of the strongest weightlifting nations at the Commonwealth Games, and Mirabai will be expected to spearhead another medal-winning day as the country looks to add to Jhandu Kumar's historic bronze.
Article Summary: Sachin Siwach beats Keoma Al-Ahmadieh 4-1 in the men's 60kg round of 32. Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh remain unbeaten in the women's lawn bowls. India's women's artistic gymnastics team finish fifth in Subdivision 3. Indian duo Dhakshan Shashikumar and Aryan Nehra miss 400m freestyle final.

Article Title: 'Aap ka beta sab jhandu kar diya': India's CWG 2026 medallist reveals the painful story behind his name 'Jhandu' Kumar
Article Text:
India's Jhandu Kumar celebrates his bronze medal. (AP Photo)

The painful story behind the name 'Jhandu'



India's Jhandu Kumar (PTI Photo)

From e-rickshaw driver to CWG medallist



Bronze today, bigger dreams tomorrow



NEW DELHI: When "Jhandu Kumar" echoed across the Commonwealth Games arena in Glasgow, it was no longer a name that invited ridicule. It was a name that had just delivered India's first medal of the 2026 Commonwealth Games.For years, Bihar's para powerlifter had endured taunts over a name born out of tragedy. On Friday, he turned that painful identity into a symbol of resilience, winning bronze in the men's heavyweight para powerlifting event and scripting one of India's most inspiring stories of the Games.The 28-year-old secured bronze with 130.9 points after successful lifts of 181kg and 190kg. A daring final attempt at 196kg, which could have pushed him into gold-medal contention, narrowly slipped away.Yet, standing on the podium, Jhandu was thinking less about the missed opportunity and more about the remarkable journey that brought him there."The happiness is overwhelming. I haven't been able to sleep since last night... Even when I lie down, sleep just doesn't come," he said during a Sports Authority of India interaction.Long before he became India's medal winner, Jhandu was a five-year-old battling polio in a small Bihar village."My family says that I got polio when I was 5 years old. I had to sit down and walk... People used to taunt me. They used to say, 'Now that he has become disabled, what will he do?'," he said.His unusual first name came from another painful chapter. His parents exhausted their savings trying to treat his illness. Family friends mocked the situation, saying, "Aap ka beta sab jhandu kar diya, sab paisa khatam kar diya" (Your son has wasted all your money).The nickname stuck. For a while, he tried to escape it by changing his name to Avinash Kumar. But during a visit to a government office, officials repeatedly called out "Jhandu Kumar."Recalling the incident, he said officials called him inside after repeatedly calling out "Jhandu Kumar" and burst into laughter when he confirmed his name. Instead of hiding from it, he chose to own it."I felt if everyone is having a good laugh at my name... then this name is good only," he said. "Now in all our documents, it is Jhandu Kumar. So, there is no existence of Avinash Kumar any more."To afford supplements and maintain his training, Jhandu spent eight to nine months driving an e-rickshaw."I drove the e-rickshaw for my diet. I thought I will earn Rs 200-400 and have supplements with that and continue my gym," he said."I used to go to gym in the evening but the problem was I used to get tired after driving all day, so gym time was getting reduced," he explained as driving was difficult because of the effects of polio.His sporting career itself began almost by chance. Initially a shot putter, he was persuaded to switch to para powerlifting by Bihar coach Kundan Pandey, who recognised his natural strength.In 2022, watching Sudhir win Commonwealth Games gold ignited a dream."When our gym owner told me Sudhir bhai had lifted 212kg and won the Commonwealth Games, I said I will also do it. I thought I have to do it for my country," he said.Jhandu approached the competition with a clear strategy: "My aim was to pass the first lift. After that, the second lift was to get into medal tally. The third lift was for the gold medal."The final attempt failed because of a technical error."I could not get the gold medal. It was a technical fault. I made a mistake in my breathing in haste. When I was going up, I did the lift right. But when I went out, it got stuck in the rack," he added.Now training at the Sports Authority of India's National Centre of Excellence in Gandhinagar, he says life remains modest back home, where his parents continue to sell vegetables.But the bronze medal is only the beginning. His ultimate ambition is already set."My journey has started. Next I have Para Asian Games and Paralympics for which I have to prepare," he said. "There is a record of 232kg. I want to break that record."
Article Summary: Bihar's Jhandu Kumar wins bronze in men's heavyweight para powerlifting event. The 28-year-old was a five-year old battling polio in a small Bihar village. His parents exhausted their savings trying to treat his illness. To afford supplements and maintain his training, he drove an e-rickshaw.

Article Title: WATCH: Gymnast Gabriel Langton suffers frightening head-first fall at CWG 2026; Team England thanks medical staff
Article Text:
England gymnast Gabriel Langton

England regroup after traumatic incident as Canada end long wait



Rivals unite in support for injured gymnast



A terrifying accident involving England gymnast Gabriel Langton cast a shadow over the men's team gymnastics final at the Commonwealth Games 2026, with a video of the horrific head-first fall quickly spreading across social media.The 19-year-old suffered the sickening crash during his high bar routine in the final rotation at The Arena in Glasgow, prompting an immediate medical response and bringing competition to a halt.Langton missed his catch on the horizontal bar, falling from around three metres and landing heavily on his head and neck. The packed arena fell into stunned silence as nearly a dozen medical personnel rushed to his aid.After receiving lengthy treatment on the competition floor, Langton was carefully placed on a stretcher, fitted with a neck brace and taken away on a trolley to a standing ovation from spectators.Team officials later confirmed he was conscious, moving his arms and legs, and speaking with doctors before being transported to hospital.The frightening incident overshadowed an otherwise historic evening for Canada, who claimed their first Commonwealth Games men's team gymnastics gold medal in 20 years.Led by all-around standout Felix Dolci, Canada finished with 241.400 points to end England's dominance in the event, while England settled for silver with 238.200.Australia secured bronze after edging hosts Scotland in a closely fought battle.Langton, who had been drafted into England's squad earlier this month to replace injured six-time Olympic medallist Max Whitlock, was unable to join his teammates on the podium following the accident.When competition resumed after the lengthy delay, England faced the difficult task of regaining focus.Luke Whitehouse, who was next to perform on the high bar, admitted the emotional challenge of continuing after witnessing his teammate's fall."When something like that happens, you've just got to forget about it and reset. I just had to focus on my routine one skill at a time," Whitehouse said.He later praised the team's resilience."We regrouped, the coaches were fantastic and the boys who had to go up on high bar were incredible. The togetherness of the team really showed."The incident prompted an outpouring of support from competitors across the field.Canada's Felix Dolci acknowledged the inherent dangers of gymnastics while paying tribute to England's composure."It's terrible. It goes to show that gymnastics is a very difficult and dangerous sport. All our thoughts go to Gabriel and the team. England stayed focused, and that's not easy after seeing something like that," Dolci said.Scotland's Hamish Carter echoed those sentiments, saying the team's thoughts were firmly with Langton."I'm just so happy that he's alright. We've walked away with no medal, but I'm thinking of Gabe in this moment," he said.Team England later issued a statement thanking the medical staff for their swift response."We are grateful to the medical teams who responded immediately to provide assistance. Gabriel has been taken to hospital and we will share more information when it is available."
Article Summary: England gymnast Gabriel Langton suffers horrific head-first fall during final rotation. 19-year-old landed heavily on his head and neck after missing his catch on the horizontal bar. Video of the incident quickly spread across social media. Canada claim first Commonwealth Games men's team gymnastics gold medal in 20 years.

Article Title: Beyond the medals at CWG 2026: IOA medical team keeps Team India fighting fit in Glasgow
Article Text:
Team India Medical Room

NEW DELHI: As India's athletes chase medals at the ongoing Commonwealth Games, an equally important contest is unfolding away from the spotlight. Behind every performance is the Indian Olympic Association's (IOA) medical team, working round the clock to ensure athletes stay fit, recover quickly and remain competition-ready through the demanding schedule.Headed by noted orthopaedic surgeon Dr Dinshaw Pardiwala, the IOA medical unit has been at work since the contingent arrived in Scotland. Assisted by physiotherapists Sumansh Sivalanka, Chris Pedra and Debashish Das, the team is overseeing injury management, physiotherapy, recovery protocols and rehabilitation across disciplines."It is a wonderful journey as my team comprising Sumansh Sivalanka, Chris Pedra and Debashish Das are working with the athletes even before the Games began.For me, personally, it is reassuring when team managers come and tell me our presence is reassuring and adds value," Dr Pardiwala said.The task has been made more challenging by the absence of a central Athletes' Village at Glasgow 2026. With the Indian contingent spread across three hotels, the IOA has set up its main treatment centre at the Mercure Hotel while deploying medical personnel at all team bases to ensure athletes have access to immediate care whenever required.The medical unit also serves smaller contingents such as swimming and gymnastics, which do not travel with dedicated doctors or physiotherapists. Larger squads, including athletics, have their own medical staff, but continue to coordinate with the IOA's central support system.For athletes competing across multiple days, recovery has become as crucial as training. Physiotherapy sessions, mobility work and rehabilitation programmes are designed to minimise injury risks while helping competitors maintain peak performance."The greatest satisfaction is to see the smile on the faces of athletes after they have had a hard day at work," Dr Pardiwala said.While medals will dominate the headlines over the coming days, every podium finish will also owe something to the doctors, physiotherapists and support staff whose work begins before the athletes step onto the field of play and often continues long after competition ends.For the IOA, the objective extends beyond medals — ensuring every Indian athlete enters competition with the confidence that a dedicated support team is standing firmly behind them.
Article Summary: Indian Olympic Association's medical team working round the clock to ensure athletes stay fit, recover quickly and remain competition-ready. Headed by noted orthopaedic surgeon Dr Dinshaw Pardiwala. Assisted by physiotherapists Sumansh Sivalanka, Chris Pedra and Debashish Das.

Article Title: CWG 2026: Rupa Rani Tirkey, Pinki Singh stay unbeaten as Indian duo closes in on women's pairs semifinals
Article Text:
India's Pinki Singh, left, and Rupa Rani Tirkey during the Women's Pairs Sectional Play. (PTI Photo)

India recover from early setback before holding nerve



Disappointment for Indian swimmers



NEW DELHI: India's women's pairs combination of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh continued its unbeaten run at the Commonwealth Games 2026, edging past Tonga in a tense tie-breaker on Saturday to move a step closer to the lawn bowls semifinals.The experienced duo, both members of India's historic women's fours team that won Commonwealth Games gold in Birmingham in 2022, defeated Tonga's Paris Baker and Milika Nathan 2-0 via a tie-breaker after the two sides shared the opening two sets in their Section B encounter.With the victory, India registered its third consecutive win in the women's pairs competition and remained firmly in the race for a semifinal berth.England also has three wins from three matches in Section B but sits atop the standings after claiming one more set than the Indian pair.Tonga made the brighter start, taking the lead after the opening end with Paris Baker producing an impressive spell that put the Indians under early pressure.Rupa, however, responded brilliantly in the second end with a superb second bowl, while skip Pinki Singh marshalled the contest expertly as India levelled the scores at 1-1.The momentum quickly shifted in India's favour as the duo combined effectively over the remaining ends to seal the opening set 5-2.The second set proved far more challenging. Baker and skip Milika Nathan dominated the early exchanges, racing to a commanding 6-0 advantage after three ends.Rupa and Pinki attempted a late recovery but were unable to erase the deficit as Tonga claimed the set 6-4, forcing the contest into a decisive tie-breaker.When the pressure was at its highest, the Indian pair delivered. Rupa gave India the early advantage before Pinki calmly finished the job, sealing another crucial victory and keeping India's unbeaten record intact.In lawn bowls, the lead is responsible for opening each end and placing bowls as close to the jack as possible, while the skip, usually the team's most experienced player, calls the tactics and delivers the final bowls of each end.It was, however, a disappointing day in the pool for India.Dhakshan Shashikumar and Aryan Nehra failed to progress to the men's 400m freestyle final after finishing outside the qualification places at the Tollcross Swimming Centre.Shashikumar clocked 3:58.09 to finish 15th overall among 27 swimmers. Competing in Heat 3, he briefly climbed to seventh position at the halfway mark but faded in the closing stages.Nehra, swimming in Heat 4, recorded 4:00.26 to place 16th overall after remaining at the back of the field throughout his race.
Article Summary: India's women's pairs combination of Rupa Rani Tirkey and Pinki Singh continued its unbeaten run at the Commonwealth Games 2026. The experienced duo defeated Tonga's Paris Baker and Milika Nathan 2-0 via a tie-breaker after the two sides shared the opening two sets in their Section B encounter. England also has three wins from three matches in Section B but sits atop the standings.

Article Title: India's para cyclist Lisha Das rejects federation's support, opts for own kit and flag
Article Text:
Lisha Das

NEW DELHI: Minor para cyclist Lisha Das escalated her dispute with the country’s sports authorities ahead of her departure for the Commonwealth Games, informing the Cycling Federation of India (CFI) that she will not wear the official India kit and will carry her own Tricolour. She also said she would stay outside the team hotel, travel on independently booked tickets and decline the federation’s travel and accommodation arrangements in Glasgow, citing “continued harassment, mental distress and lack of support”.In another strongly worded email — a copy of which is with TOI — the athlete demanded immediate accreditation and field-of-play access for her coach, Aditya Mehta, saying the Delhi high court had already recognised him as her coach. She reiterated that Mehta, technician K Dattatraya and physiotherapist Dr Asha Shaikh must be granted the necessary event access as her essential support personnel.Lisha also objected to the use of her photographs on official platforms of the Paralympic Committee of India (PCI), alleging that they created a misleading impression that she had been trained, sponsored or supported by the authorities. As a minor, she said neither she nor her guardian had consented to the use of the photographs and warned of legal action if thematerial was not removed.Her latest communication came after the CFI informed her that it had booked flight tickets for Lisha, Dr Shaikh and Dattatraya and was arranging accreditation, accommodation and airport transfers for the Indian para-cycling contingent in Glasgow. Mehta, however, was not included as her coach.Rejecting the arrangements, Lisha wrote, “I will not be wearing the official kit. I will be wearing my own kit and carrying my own Indian flag.”She said she had independently borne the expenses for her training, equipment and Games participation. According to her coaching team, the expenditure amounted to around Rs 12 lakh, including non-refundable flight tickets, private accommodation in Glasgow and customs duty paid on her high-end customised cycle.Lisha added that she saw no reason to represent a support system “from whom I have not received meaningful support”. She further claimed that the federation had booked tickets “without informing me in advance” and that her coach and support team had already finalised their travel and accommodation because of the “prolonged lack of clarity and timely communication”.Stressing that she would continue to represent India with pride, Lisha maintained that her independent arrangements should not dilute her demand for accreditation for Mehta and her support staff.
Article Summary: Minor para cyclist Lisha Das escalated her dispute with the country’s sports authorities ahead of her departure for the Commonwealth Games. She has informed the Cycling Federation of India that she will not wear the official India kit and will carry her own Tricolour. She also said she would stay outside the team hotel, travel on independently booked tickets and decline the federation's travel and accommodation arrangements.
